=== #595 ===
[OPEN] Scale-aware execution: sampling / partition-aware checks for the flat-file + UC runners (G-b)
Gap G-b (post-v1-roadmap maturity assessment) — the flat-file + UC runners load the whole file/table into worker pandas; a 100M-row table = worker OOM. The Snowflake path pushes down via SQL and is fine (reference baseline captured in #587 before the subscription lapsed).

**Scope (named workstream under Theme 7):**
- **Row-cap / sampling strategy** per suite or per run-target: head-N, random-sample, and (flat-file) per-file/partition batching via the existing batch-resolution machinery — with the sampled-ness recorded on the result (a check that passed on a sample must say so).
- **UC:** push what's pushable down to Spark/SQL before collecting (freshness/volume/schema_drift monitors never need the full table; expectation subsets that can run as SQL should).
- **Guardrail:** a size probe + configurable hard cap so the worker refuses-with-`error` instead of OOMing.
- **Perf batch same week:** #327 (profiler N+1) + #323 (retention-sweep index/batch) — same theme, same harness.
- Testable cloud-independently: local files at parameterized volume (HARNESS_TODO §6 generator) + Databricks Free for UC.

Incremental (delta-only) validation stays a follow-up — design it, don't build it here.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Sampling strategies (head-N / random) + per-partition/file batching for the flat-file runner; UC pushes monitors + SQL-able subsets down before any collect
- [ ] Size probe + configurable hard cap → run ends `error` with a clear message instead of worker OOM
- [ ] Sampled-ness recorded on the result and visible in the UI (a pass on a sample says so)
- [ ] Volume test vs the #587 Snowflake baseline documented

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #327 ===
[OPEN] perf(profiler): batch the N+1 per-column top-values warehouse queries
Split out of #147 (item 4) so that issue can close — the other four cleanup items are resolved/confirmed there.

`profile_table` ([profile_service.py](backend/app/services/profile_service.py)) issues 1 aggregate query + **one top-values query per column** in a Python loop. For a 50-column profile that's 51 sequential warehouse round-trips; against a cold SQL warehouse (~1s/query) that's ~50s of wall time for an interactive authoring aid.

Acceptable for v1 (≤50-col cap, and the aggregate query is a single round-trip), so this is **post-v1 perf**, not a correctness bug.

### Why not done now
- Explicitly conditional in #147: "consider batching … **if profiler latency becomes a problem**."
- A safe rewrite (e.g. `UNION ALL` of per-column grouped+limited subqueries, one round-trip) mixes differently-typed `value` columns into one projection, which coerces per-dialect — genuinely risky across both Snowflake and Databricks, and **live warehouse runs are still the deferred Week-1 smoke**, so there's no integration test to catch a regression.

### When to pick up
Once a live warehouse smoke exists (so the batched SQL can be validated end-to-end), or if profiler latency is reported in practice. Keep the per-column builder as the fallback for dialects where the batched form misbehaves.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Profiler top-values collected in batched queries (O(1)–O(2) per table, not per column)
- [ ] Before/after timing recorded; behavior unchanged (tests)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #323 ===
[OPEN] Index + batch the result-retention sweep for large results tables
Follow-up from the A8 result-retention sweep (`run_service.purge_expired_sample_failures`, daily `purge_sample_failures` beat task). Surfaced by `/code-review` on the retention PR. Functionality is correct and tested; these are scale optimizations deferred to keep the PR to one functionality.

### 1. No index supports the sweep predicate
The daily `UPDATE results SET sample_failures=NULL, sample_failures_purged_at=now WHERE created_at < cutoff AND sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) NOT IN (NULL,'null')` filters on `created_at` + `sample_failures_purged_at`, but `results.__table_args__` indexes only `run_id` and `check_id`. `results` grows by one row per check per run with no row-delete (ADR 0012 keeps `metric_value`), so the sweep does a full sequential scan of an unbounded table every day to scrub a small set.

**Fix:** a backward-compatible Alembic migration adding a partial index, e.g.
`CREATE INDEX ix_results_unpurged_created ON results (created_at) WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL;`
(tested up/down locally per the migration checklist). The partial predicate keeps the index tiny — it only covers not-yet-purged rows.

### 2. First run on an aged DB does one large unbounded UPDATE
The sweep is a single `UPDATE ... WHERE` with no `LIMIT`/batching. On first run after enabling retention (or after a long outage), it can rewrite a large backlog in one transaction — long row locks + WAL/dead-tuple pressure, briefly contending with concurrent result inserts. The schedule dispatcher deliberately processes one row at a time with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` to avoid exactly this.

**Fix:** batch the purge (e.g. loop `UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id ... LIMIT N)` until 0 rows) so each transaction is bounded. Steady-state matches are small, so this only matters for the catch-up run.

### Not changed (intentional)
- `synchronize_session=False` was already applied on the PR (the `auto`→`fetch` fallback was emitting an extra SELECT-of-PKs).

_Filed per the working agreement: review findings deferred from a PR are tracked, never silently dropped._

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Retention sweep uses an index + batched deletes/updates; runtime on a large seeded `results` table measured
- [ ] No lock-contention regression (documented check)

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #318 ===
[OPEN] Run progress is binary 0%→100% (GX atomic batch) — no true per-check incremental progress
Surfaced during the /code-review of PR #315 (live run-progress drawer, A3). Pre-existing limitation, not introduced by that PR — filing so it isn't lost.

`run_service.get_run_progress` derives `completed_checks`/`counts` from the presence of `Result` rows. Because GX validates a suite in **one atomic batch**, all result rows land together at completion — so for any non-trivial suite the live-progress bar reads `0 / N` (0%) for the entire run, then jumps to `N / N` (100%) at the terminal transition. The endpoint reports **lifecycle + final per-check resolution**, not sub-GX incremental progress (documented in the `get_run_progress` docstring).

This contradicts the UX intent the consuming code advertises ("watches it execute check-by-check" — [Suites.tsx](frontend/src/pages/Suites.tsx) onRun comment): a long run will read as hung at 0% until it finishes.

**Options (all post-v1, non-trivial):**
- Per-check execution (split the GX batch / run validations incrementally) so rows land as checks complete — biggest change, touches the runner.
- A spinner-only "running" affordance for multi-check suites instead of a 0% bar, to avoid the "hung" read.
- Surface an elapsed-time / heartbeat instead of a misleading percentage while `completed_checks == 0`.

Tie-in: the `freshness`/`volume` monitor-kinds (ADR 0012) and any non-GX runner may not be atomic-batch, so a per-runner progress contract is the deeper fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Run progress reports per-check/per-partition increments instead of binary 0%→100% (natural once #595's partitioned execution lands — ride that work)
- [ ] Live-progress drawer reflects the increments; progress endpoint contract unchanged or versioned
- [ ] Tests cover multi-partition progress sequencing

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

=== #310 ===
[OPEN] decision (ADR): history/audit strategy — check-version history lost on delete, no audit log, no soft-delete
## Context

The internal Postgres data has **no general SCD/history framework** — it's Alembic for schema + targeted mechanisms. The history/audit review found:

1. **Check version history is lost on delete.** `check_versions.check_id` is `ondelete=CASCADE`, so deleting a check (or a suite, which cascades to its checks) wipes its entire `check_versions` history. History survives *edits* (SCD Type 4) but not *deletion*.
2. **No general audit log.** `connections` (credential/config changes), `shares` (grant/revoke), `trigger_bindings` are SCD Type 1 (overwrite + `updated_at`) or hard-deleted with no who/when/before/after trail.
3. **All deletes are hard deletes** (`session.delete`) — no soft-delete (`deleted_at`) anywhere. A deleted connection orphans the meaning of past runs ("what did this run actually check?").
4. **No SCD Type 2** (`valid_from`/`valid_to` versioned dimensions) anywhere.

## Decision needed (ADR)

Pick the history/audit posture for v1.x+:
- **(a)** Preserve check history on delete — `check_versions.check_id` → `RESTRICT`/`SET NULL` + self-contained identity, or a tombstone.
- **(b)** Soft-delete (`deleted_at`) for `connections`/`suites` so run lineage survives.
- **(c)** A single cross-entity **audit log** (`actor, entity_type, entity_id, action, before, after, ts`) — cheaper/uniform vs per-table versioning; covers connections/shares/triggers that have no history today.
- **(d)** Full SCD Type 2 on selected dimensions (heaviest — see the cost analysis on this issue).

## Acceptance
- [ ] ADR recording the chosen posture + rationale + which entities get which treatment
- [ ] Follow-up implementation issue(s) per the decision (e.g. the `check_versions` ondelete fix is small and could be pulled forward)

## Context
From the history/SCD review. Single-tenant v1 likely doesn't need full SCD2, but the check-history-on-delete (1) is a near-term correctness item worth deciding deliberately.


## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] ADR merged deciding the history/audit remainder: cross-entity audit log + soft-delete — accepted or explicitly re-deferred with rationale
- [ ] Consistent with the #596 G-d design and #431; follow-up issues filed if accepted

_(AC added at v1.1 planning, 2026-07-04.)_

input.prompt:
You are implementing GitHub issue #327 in the DataQ repo (TheurgicDuke771/DataQ). You are in an isolated git worktree of /Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ — work there, branch off main as `perf/issue-327-profiler-batch-topvalues`.

FIRST read: CLAUDE.md (root), CONTRIBUTING.md, `gh issue view 327`. Then the code: backend/app/services/profile_service.py (`profile_table` — 1 aggregate query + one top-values query per column in a Python loop), backend/app/datasources/sql.py (shared SQL-identifier allowlist), and how the profiler's queries are built/executed per datasource (SQLAlchemy Core builders — note #937: quoting must come from the CONNECTION's dialect, never hand-rolled; UC uses backticks, Snowflake double-quotes).

SCOPE: collapse the N+1 per-column top-values round-trips into O(1)–O(2) batched queries per table (e.g. UNION ALL of per-column grouped+limited subqueries, with each value projected as a CAST to a common type or per-column marker columns — the issue warns mixed-type `value` projection coerces per-dialect). Requirements:
- Build with SQLAlchemy Core so each dialect quotes/renders itself; NO hand-rolled quoting, no f-string SQL.
- KEEP the per-column builder as an explicit fallback path (the issue mandates it) — e.g. if the batched query fails, log + fall back per-column so a dialect quirk degrades to the old behavior instead of breaking the profiler.
- Behavior unchanged: same top-values output per column (ordering, ties, null handling). Lock this with tests that run the REAL generated SQL against a real local Postgres (see how backend/tests does this for custom SQL — "standing in for the warehouse"), plus unit tests for the builder including adversarial column names (case-sensitive, reserved words, spaces).
- Record before/after timing (seeded local Postgres table with ~30-50 columns is fine) in the PR body per the AC.
- IMPORTANT caveat for the PR body: per this repo's #953 rule, cross-dialect SQL is only proven by a live warehouse run — state explicitly that live Snowflake + Unity Catalog verification is PENDING and will be done by the orchestrator before the issue is considered fully verified. Do not claim dialect correctness beyond what your tests prove.

HARD RULES: conventional commits, one functionality per commit; local verification BEFORE push from conda env `dataq` (`conda run -n dataq ...`; Fish shell — quote globs, no `timeout`, avoid `cd &&`): Black --check, Ruff, mypy, Bandit, pytest; mutation-check regression tests (prove they fail against the old code where meaningful); `git merge origin/main` if main moved (never force-push); commits end with: Co-Authored-By: Claude Fable 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

Repo state checked and the Week 6 close-out is now in motion. Here's the picture and the plan:

## Current state

- `main` is clean and up to date; v1.1 W1–W5 are closed, plus the OTP track and several unplanned batches.
- **W6 milestone ("scale-aware execution + hardening + cycle close", due 2026-08-14)** is at 95 closed / 6 open. Most of the original 14-task table is already done (#563, #573, #278, #322, #571, #541, #306, #457, and the W6-adjacent #1200/#1202/#1203 are all closed).

## What's actually pending

| Priority | Task | Why / dependency |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [#595](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/595) Scale-aware execution (sampling + partition batching + OOM guardrail, flat-file + UC) | **P1, the W6 exit-gate anchor** |
| 2 | [#323](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/323) Retention-sweep partial index + batched purge | Independent, migration involved |
| 3 | [#310](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/310) History/audit strategy ADR + follow-up issues | Decision doc, feeds the W7 compliance track |
| 4 | [#327](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/327) Profiler N+1 top-values batching | Independent; dialect-risky SQL → live-verify before close |
| 5 | [#318](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/issues/318) Per-check incremental run progress | **Blocked on #595** (rides its partitioned execution) — queued |
| 6 | Cycle retro + `v1.1.0` tag + docs close-out | Last, after everything merges |

## Execution now running

I've delegated a batch of four agents in isolated worktrees (per the standing batch-size agreement):

- **#595 → Opus** — the complex one: sampling strategies, UC pushdown, size-probe hard cap (fixing the #755 silent-OOM-hang), sampled-ness recorded on results, volume test vs the #587 baseline.
- **#323 → Sonnet** — partial index migration (up+down tested) + bounded-transaction batched purge with measurements.
- **#310 → Opus** — ADR deciding options (a)–(d) against the actual codebase, consistent with ADR 0034 and the W7 #431 compliance issue, with follow-up issues filed.
- **#327 → Opus** — Core-built batched top-values query with the per-column fallback retained; flagged that live Snowflake/UC verification stays with me before the issue closes (the #953 rule).

Each opens a PR without merging. When they report back I'll run `/code-review` on every PR, fix or file findings, merge sequentially, then launch #318 (+ sampled-ness UI surfacing) on top of #595, and finish with the retro + `v1.1.0` tag. I'll report as each lands.

## Deliverables

**PR:** [#1321](https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1321) — `docs: ADR 0041 — history/audit strategy (#310)`, `Fixes #310`, milestone *v1.1 Week 6*, CI **16/16 green**, not merged.
**ADR number: 0041** (`docs/adr/0041-history-audit-strategy.md`) — 0020 already existed on this topic and deferred exactly the remainder #310's v1.1 AC asks about, so 0041 **amends 0020** rather than restating it. Per the README `Amends` rule I also added the amendment blockquote to 0020 and the `(amended by 0041 — …)` note on its index Status.

## Decisions

- **(c) cross-entity audit log — ACCEPTED.** One append-only `audit_events` table. `entity_id` deliberately carries **no FK** (an FK either cascades the audit row away or blocks the delete) — that's what lets it answer what a Type-4 table structurally cannot: the delete event. **#431/G1 is phase 2 on the same table** via an `action_class` discriminant, not a second table, with the *opposite* latency contract (phase 1 writes inside the mutation's transaction, fail-closed; phase-2 reads must stay off the critical path — #431's own call).
- **(a) preserve check-version history on delete — REJECTED as stated; need met by (c).** `RESTRICT` makes every check undeletable, `SET NULL` orphans rows needing self-contained identity (a worse audit log scoped to one entity), tombstone = soft-delete for one table. Cascade now stands for a *positive* reason.
- **(b) soft-delete — RE-DEFERRED,** on a narrower argument than 0020's. Its headline motivation is already dead: #753/#541 made `delete_connection` 409 while dependents exist, so a connection can no longer be deleted out from under its runs — #310's claim 3 is half stale. Remaining reasons: the column is trivial next to "deleted means inert" for live credentials/bindings/schedules, and a delete-that-doesn't-delete fights #432 Art-17 erasure.
- **(d) SCD-2 — CLOSED permanently,** not deferred.

Redaction is addressed in §2.6, including a sharp one: `_PII_KEYS` contains `name`/`display_name`/`user_id`, so reusing the logger redactor wholesale would strip the *content of a rename event* and the actor label — payloads use per-entity allow-lists plus only the credential subset, and never `sample_failures`/`observed_value` in either phase.

## Follow-ups filed (all *v1.1 Backlog*, referenced by number from the ADR)

- **#1318** — phase-1 build (P2, enhancement+security)
- **#1319** — three `created_by` FKs still have no `ondelete`; residue of #541's user half, live the moment #432 lands (P3, bug)
- **#1320** — suite-delete blast-radius confirmation, the mitigation that makes rejecting (b) honest (P3)

Also posted a scope note on **#431** so nobody builds a second table in W7.

## One thing worth flagging

The mandated `/code-review` found a **blocker**: my §1 asserted ADR 0033 "made roles a stored, mutable `users.role`" — it doesn't exist (0033 is accepted but unbuilt, #740–#744). Plus three MAJORs, including that I'd overclaimed the `REVOKE` as tamper-resistance when `dataq_app` **owns** the table and can re-grant, and that splitting the role would violate the standing single-role Postgres constraint. All 12 findings are fixed in `d995935a`, dispositions posted to the PR, and #1318's body corrected so the implementer doesn't inherit the overclaims. Nothing deferred.</result>

<result>Reviewed the diff, migration, and `run_service.py` 1276–1465 in the worktree. All the flagged efficiency problems are real and verifiable from the code. Six findings, ordered by severity.

## Finding 1 — Index docstring claim is false: the partial index retains every passing-check row forever

**File:** `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` lines 20–26 (same claim repeated in `backend/app/db/models.py` lines 862–866, "small, shrinking working set")

**Summary:** "the index only ever covers the sweep's actual working set, not the whole table" does not hold — the index asymptotically covers ~the whole table.

**Failure scenario:** A row leaves the partial index only when `sample_failures_purged_at` is stamped. But the first purge half's `jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) IS NOT NULL AND != 'null'` guard (run_service.py:1427–1429) permanently excludes every row whose `sample_failures` is SQL NULL — i.e. **every passing check's result, the majority of the table** — so those rows are never stamped and never leave the index. The index therefore grows linearly with total results written, dominated by never-eligible entries. Concretely: every daily sweep's index range scan (`created_at < cutoff` covers all history) must heap-fetch every one of those dead entries to evaluate the typeof guards (typeof can't be answered from an index storing only `created_at`), so the daily sweep is O(all historical passing rows) every day — not O(the day's expired crop) as the migration claims. The index only excludes already-purged rows, the *minority* on a passing-dominated table, so the headline perf claim of the PR largely evaporates.

**Fix:** put the typeof guards into the index predicate — `WHERE sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL AND sample_failures IS NOT NULL AND jsonb_typeof(sample_failures) <> 'null'` — which the sweep's predicate still implies. Then never-eligible rows never enter the index, and it genuinely shrinks to the working set.

## Finding 2 — Batched loop re-scans the ever-growing dead prefix per chunk: catch-up is superlinear

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1329–1347

**Summary:** Each chunk's `SELECT id ... LIMIT chunk_size` restarts the index scan from the bottom of the `created_at` range, re-skipping all never-eligible entries every iteration — no keyset progression.

**Failure scenario:** Never-eligible (passing-row) entries below cutoff don't shrink between iterations (Finding 1), and eligible entries interleave with them by `created_at`. Chunk *k* must skip past roughly `k·chunk_size·(P/E)` dead entries (P = never-eligible rows below cutoff, E = eligible backlog) before assembling its 500 IDs, each skip a heap fetch to evaluate the typeof filter. Summed over `B = E/500` chunks that is **~P·E/1000 heap fetches**. Concrete: P = 2M passing rows, E = 100k backlog → ~2×10⁸ row visits across 200 chunks, versus the pre-PR single seq scan visiting ~2.1M rows once — the "catch-up run … which is precisely the case the AC's 'no lock-contention regression' check targets" (comment at 1281–1284) is exactly the case this makes ~100× *worse* in total I/O. Fixing the index predicate (Finding 1) collapses this, since purged rows then leave the index and each rescan starts at the first live entry; keyset pagination (`ORDER BY created_at, id` + resume-after cursor) is the belt-and-braces alternative.

## Finding 3 — The observed_value half cannot use the new index at all; batching turned 1 full scan into N full scans

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1438–1445

**Summary:** The second half's predicate (`created_at < cutoff AND jsonb_typeof(observed_value->'observed_value') = 'array'`) has no `sample_failures_purged_at IS NULL` term, so it does not imply the partial index's predicate — Postgres will never use `ix_results_unpurged_created` for it. There is no other `created_at` index.

**Failure scenario:** Every chunk of the observed_value half is a sequential scan (LIMIT lets early chunks stop early, but the final iteration — which always runs, that's the loop's exit condition — scans the entire table). For an observed_value catch-up backlog of E rows, the pre-PR code did exactly **one** full scan; this PR does up to **⌈E/500⌉ + 1** full scans. The PR regressed the very half it claims to have indexed. Fix: a second partial index `ON results (created_at) WHERE jsonb_typeof(observed_value->'observed_value') = 'array'` — small by construction (only set-oriented expectations produce the array shape) and exactly implied by this half's predicate.

## Finding 4 — `_purge_column` docstring's "index makes the extra scan pass cheap" is a broken perf claim

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1313–1314

**Summary:** The justification for keeping two separate UPDATEs ("The daily 01:17 UTC cadence and the `ix_results_unpurged_created` partial index (#323) make the extra scan pass cheap") is false for one of the two passes.

**Failure scenario:** The "extra scan pass" being excused is precisely the observed_value UPDATE — the one that cannot use the index (Finding 3) and seq-scans daily. The rationale recorded in the code for an architectural choice (two UPDATEs vs one CASE-based UPDATE) rests on an index benefit that doesn't exist for that pass; the next person reading this will wrongly believe both halves are indexed. Either add the second partial index or correct the claim.

## Finding 5 — Extra empty round-trip when backlog is an exact multiple of chunk_size

**File:** `backend/app/services/run_service.py` lines 1342–1346

**Summary:** Exit sentinel is `affected < chunk_size`, so a backlog of exactly `k·chunk_size` runs one additional iteration that selects and updates nothing.

**Failure scenario:** The wasted iteration is not just a round-trip: for the observed_value half it is **one additional full sequential scan of `results`** (Finding 3), and for the sample_failures half one additional full walk of the dead index prefix (Finding 2) — the emptiest iteration is the most expensive one, because finding zero matching rows means exhausting the entire candidate range. Also note the loop *always* runs at least once even when nothing is eligible (steady state for the observed_value half most days is 0 rows → a daily full seq scan to conclude "nothing to do" — pre-existing shape, but the PR's docstrings now describe it as cheap). Cheap mitigation for the multiple-of-chunk case: run the SELECT first and skip the UPDATE when it returns no IDs, or exit on `affected == 0` after a `chunk_size`-sized batch only when a follow-up probe is free — but the real fix is the indexes above, which make the empty pass cheap for real.

## Finding 6 — The new index disables HOT updates for the purge and taxes every result insert

**File:** `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` line 70–71 (index definition)

**Summary:** Two standing costs the migration docstring doesn't account: (a) `sample_failures_purged_at` now appears in an index *predicate*, so every purge UPDATE is HOT-disqualified; (b) every result INSERT (all new rows have `purged_at` NULL) must add an entry to this index.

**Failure scenario:** (a) Before this PR no index referenced `sample_failures` or `sample_failures_purged_at`, so purge UPDATEs could be HOT — heap-only, no index maintenance. Now each purged row writes new index tuples into `ix_results_run_id`, `ix_results_check_id`, and the new index, tripling per-row write amplification on exactly the bulk operation the PR set out to lighten. (b) The insert-path tax funds an index whose entries, per Finding 1, mostly never earn their keep (never-eligible passing rows sit in it forever). Both costs become acceptable — small index, few entries — once the typeof guards move into the index predicate (Finding 1's fix), because then passing-row inserts skip the index entirely and only sample-bearing rows pay. As shipped, the hottest write path in the system (`results` insert, one per check per run) pays for an index that doesn't deliver its claimed benefit.

---

**Bottom line for the PR's perf claims:** the batching-for-lock-bounding part is sound in shape, but the index as specified doesn't deliver the claimed working-set bound (Finding 1), the chunk loop makes catch-up sweeps asymptotically *worse* than the single UPDATE it replaced (Findings 2, 3), and the second purge half is entirely unindexed despite docstrings implying otherwise (Findings 3, 4). The coherent fix is one index-predicate change plus one additional partial index; both are implied by the sweeps' own WHERE clauses and require no code change in `_purge_column`.</result>

- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1439-1445 (second `_purge_column` call); also the migration docstring at `backend/alembic/versions/fbf4fe92e295_add_results_unpurged_created_index.py` lines 26-32.

- Failure scenario: a catch-up backlog of M eligible observed_value rows now costs `ceil(M/500)+1` sequential scans of the unbounded table (each chunk's `SELECT id ... LIMIT 500` subquery restarts the scan; previously-purged rows no longer match, so every scan re-reads the prefix), versus exactly **one** scan pre-PR. **2. Atomicity loss → permanent undercount in the audit log / return value.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1343 (`session.commit()` per chunk) vs. the log emission at line 1455.
- Old invariant: one transaction covering both purges + a log line whose counts exactly equaled the durable effect — a failure meant zero rows purged and a complete retry next day. New: an exception or worker death at chunk k leaves chunks 1..k-1 durably purged, the `sample_failures_purged` event never fires, and the task returns nothing. Because purged rows self-exclude (`purged_at` stamped / column nulled), the **next** sweep's counts exclude them too — so those rows never appear in any log event, ever.
- Failure scenario: anything keying off this event's `purged`/`total_purged` (the docstring at 1451-1454 explicitly protects such consumers) permanently under-reports after any mid-sweep failure; a PII-audit reconciling "rows scrubbed" against log history now has an unexplainable gap. Not re-established anywhere in the new code; at minimum a per-chunk progress log (or logging inside `_purge_column`) would restore accounting.

**3. Cross-column consistency window between the two halves.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, lines 1423-1445.
- Old: both column purges became visible atomically at the caller's single commit. New: half 1's chunks commit while half 2 hasn't run; a worker death between the calls leaves rows `sample_failures`-purged but with the PII-bearing `observed_value` array intact until the next beat (~25h extra exposure of exactly the data the sweep exists to remove — and half 2 is the slow, index-less half per finding 1, widening the window). Readers meanwhile see the intermediate state; mitigated for *display* by #1115's read-time "partial" redaction state, but the PII-retention SLA half-miss is real and unlogged (finding 2 compounds it).

**4. A helper now commits a caller-owned session — contract change invisible in the signature.**
- File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1343.
- Old: `_purge_column` was pure DML; the sole commit was the caller's, so a caller could compose the purge into a larger transaction and roll everything back. New: the loop unconditionally commits at least once (even a zero-affected first iteration), flushing **any** pending caller state at the first chunk boundary. Current callers are safe (beat task = fresh session; tests = savepoint fixture), so this is latent, but the failure scenario is nameable: a future caller that writes its own row (audit entry, admin-triggered purge record) before calling `purge_expired_sample_failures` has that write committed mid-helper, and its later `rollback()` becomes a silent no-op. - File: `backend/app/services/run_service.py`, line 1345.

The new loop treats `rowcount < chunk_size` as "candidate set exhausted" — but `rowcount` counts rows actually updated, and results rows **are** row-deleted in prod via the suite-delete FK cascade (#540/#542). Under READ COMMITTED, if a concurrent suite delete commits while a chunk's UPDATE runs, EvalPlanQual skips the deleted rows, so the subquery can select 500 ids while the UPDATE reports, say, 480 — the loop breaks with eligible rows still beyond the LIMIT.
- Failure scenario: a suite deletion concurrent with a catch-up sweep silently truncates that day's purge; expired PII survives an extra day, and (per finding 2's shape) nothing logs that the sweep stopped early. Self-heals next day, so severity is low, but the sentinel would be robust as `if affected == 0: break` (termination still guaranteed by the monotonic self-exclusion the docstring itself relies on) at the cost of one extra empty iteration.

**F3 — CIC retry trap: a cancelled `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` leaves an INVALID index that `IF NOT EXISTS` silently accepts.** `alembic/env.py` sets `lock_timeout=15s` engine-wide, and CIC's wait phases are ordinary lock waits — the migrate job runs while the old revision's beat/GX runs still write `results`, so a >15s writer cancels the CIC. Retry then no-ops on the INVALID index and stamps head; prod permanently carries an index the planner never uses, with zero signal. **Fix:** `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY IF EXISTS` immediately before each CREATE inside the same `autocommit_block()` (self-healing retry), for both indexes.

**F4 — loop exit `affected < chunk_size` has two failure modes.** (a) `chunk_size=0` (public kwarg, unvalidated): `LIMIT 0` → `affected=0` → `0 < 0` False → infinite empty UPDATE+commit loop occupying the worker slot. (b) Concurrent suite-delete FK-cascades (#540/#542) delete selected rows mid-chunk; EPQ skips them, `affected = 500−k < 500`, loop breaks with the remaining backlog stranded until tomorrow, unlogged. **Fix:** exit on `affected == 0` (termination stays guaranteed by monotonic self-exclusion; costs one empty iteration — cheap once F1/F2 land) + a `chunk_size >= 1` guard.

**F5 — EPQ re-stamp race: the guards moved out of the UPDATE's own WHERE.** The outer UPDATE is `WHERE id IN (subquery)` only; under READ COMMITTED an overlapping sweep's EPQ recheck re-evaluates just the id-set and re-stamps `sample_failures_purged_at` with a later timestamp (audit-value corruption + double-count). Unrealistic today (single embedded beat, max_replicas=1) but one `az` scale command away. **Fix:** repeat `created_at < cutoff` + the `extra_where` guards on the outer UPDATE.

**F6 — second hand-rolled chunked-DML copy, already diverged.** The loop mirrors `asset_service.sweep_orphan_assets` (the comment even argues "one shared convention") but drops its `rowcount or 0` guard — a `-1` rowcount driver returns a negative total and breaks the sentinel. F4's fix would otherwise need two coordinated edits. **Fix:** extract one shared `chunked_dml(...)` helper (services/ or db/ util) + one shared chunk constant; apply the `affected == 0` exit + `or 0` there, and point `sweep_orphan_assets` at it.

### Should-fix (minor)
- **M1** Mid-sweep failure now leaves committed purges with no `sample_failures_purged` event, ever (purged rows self-exclude from the next day's counts) — log per-chunk or emit running totals in a `finally`.
- **M2** `ORDER BY created_at` on the candidate SELECT — free, oldest-first is the right PII-retention order, and it removes the deadlock footgun if the single-beat assumption ever changes.
- **M3** PR title `perf:` is outside the repo's closed conventional-commit vocabulary (CONTRIBUTING rule 10 lists exactly seven; zero `perf:` commits on main) — retitle `fix:` or `refactor:` before squash.
- **M4** Dead trailing `session.commit()` + its 3-line justification in `purge_expired_sample_failures` — nothing can be pending there; drop both.
- **M5** `test_batches_across_multiple_chunks_purge_everything` is subsumed by the batch-count test + `test_scrubs_old_rows_keeps_metric`; fold its refresh-assertions in and delete.

### File (not this PR)
- The migration-parity literal-set check compares `∅ == ∅` for literal-free predicates — an inverted `IS NULL`/`IS NOT NULL` on either side keeps parity green. Worth a small hardening issue.

### Verified-benign (recorded, no change)
Mid-helper commits are safe for both real callers (fresh task session; `create_savepoint` test fixture); revision chain/head is sound, no id collision; model-side `postgresql_where` keeps `create_all` DBs schema-equal; both halves' values provably self-exclude so the loop terminates; the batch-count test's expected 4 UPDATEs is arithmetically right and was genuinely mutation-verified; two-overlapping-sweeps under-count was assessed unrealistic (it over-counts instead — F5 covers the residue).

## Batching design — and how mixed types are handled

**A rank driver LEFT-joined to one derived table per column**, not a `UNION ALL`:

```sql
SELECT r.rn, t0.value AS v_0, t0.freq AS f_0, t1.value AS v_1, t1.freq AS f_1, …
FROM (SELECT 1 AS rn UNION ALL SELECT 2 AS rn …) AS dq_ranks r
LEFT JOIN (SELECT ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0) AS rn,
                  c0 AS value, count(*) AS freq
           FROM tbl WHERE c0 IS NOT NULL GROUP BY c0
           ORDER BY count(*) DESC, c0 LIMIT n) AS dq_top_0 ON dq_top_0.rn = r.rn
LEFT JOIN (…) AS dq_top_1 ON dq_top_1.rn = r.rn
ORDER BY r.rn
```

Each derived table is *exactly* the query `build_top_values_query` already built, plus a `ROW_NUMBER()` on the same ordering expression — which is both the join key and what restores per-column order (ties included) without re-sorting values in Python, where string collation wouldn't match the warehouse's. All SQLAlchemy Core; the connection's dialect quotes everything.

**Mixed types are handled by never unifying them** — each column keeps its own output column and its own type, so NUMERIC arrives as `Decimal` and TIMESTAMP as a datetime.

**The `UNION ALL` shape was built first and is the trap the issue flagged.** A union unifies branch types, so all values land in one `value` projection (Postgres refuses `integer`/`text`; Snowflake silently coerces to `VARCHAR`). Per-column value slots padded with `NULL` **do not rescue it**: an untyped `NULL` resolves pairwise left-to-right, so in a left-deep union tree two padding slots settle on `text` before the branch owning the slot is reached — Postgres rejected it with `UNION types text and timestamp without time zone cannot be matched`. It compiled cleanly and passed every SQL-text assertion; only running it found it.

Chunk size `_TOP_VALUES_BATCH = 25` is **measured**: on 50 cols × 50k rows the pass held ~270 ms at every chunk from 8–25 and jumped to ~820 ms as a single 50-way join (Postgres switches to its genetic optimiser at 12 relations). 25 puts the endpoint's own 50-column cap at exactly 2 batched round-trips.

## Fallback semantics

Any exception from a batch → the whole set is re-collected column-by-column via `_top_values_per_column` (kept as live code), logging `profile_top_values_batch_fallback` with the exception type so a perpetually-falling-back warehouse is visible rather than merely slow. A `DataQError` (bad identifier) is re-raised untouched, not retried. `top_n < 1` routes directly to the per-column path; an empty column list issues nothing. If the retry also fails, the pre-existing 502 is unchanged.

## Before/after (real seams, seeded local Postgres, 50k rows, top_n=10)

| columns | round-trips | local median | +50 ms/RT | +250 ms/RT | +1000 ms/RT |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 30 → **2** | 152 → 140 ms | 1.98 → **0.28 s** | 7.99 → **0.69 s** | 30.51 → **2.16 s** (14.1×) |
| 40 | 40 → **2** | 193 → 189 ms | 2.67 → **0.31 s** | 10.54 → **0.70 s** | 40.46 → **2.25 s** (18.0×) |
| 50 | 50 → **2** | 276 → 263 ms | 3.34 → **0.39 s** | 13.46 → **0.81 s** | 50.85 → **2.27 s** (22.4×) |

Every run asserted `batched == per-column` before timing.

## Tests

- **New live-Postgres module** (`test_profile_batched_top_values_pg.py`, skips without `TEST_DATABASE_URL`): asserts **equivalence, not plausibility** — batched vs per-column equal in values *and* `type()` (so `10.5` can't pass for `Decimal('10.50')`), count tie-break, per-column `top_n`, native NUMERIC/TIMESTAMP, short-column LEFT-JOIN padding, all-null columns, and an identical end-to-end `ProfileResult` on batched vs forced-fallback. Adversarial-but-legal names: `Status`, `ORDER_TS`, `amount$usd`.
- **Unit tests**: SQL shape, rank driver, fragment-equivalence with the per-column builder, mixed-case quoting, 3-part UC namespace, injection-shaped identifiers, both guard rails, collector behaviour.
- **Endpoint tests**: round-trip count (12 cols → 2 executes), chunking arithmetic, fallback path.
- **Found and fixed a silent coverage hole**: `_FakeConn` understood only the old shape, so every endpoint test was passing *through the fallback* — green while covering a path production doesn't take.
- **Mutation-checked: 10/10 mutations killed** (dropped rn sort, dropped tie-break, no fallback, never batch, padding-as-data, ignored chunk size, no outer ORDER BY, rank from 0, INNER join, dropped IS NOT NULL).
- Local battery: Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit + **3955 passed, 1 skipped, 97.18% coverage**.

## ⚠️ Pending live verification (stated in the PR body, progress.md and CLAUDE.md)

Per the **#953 rule**, the batched SQL is **proven on PostgreSQL only**. Snowflake and Unity Catalog acceptance is **NOT proven and not claimed** — `ORDER BY … LIMIT` in a derived table, `ROW_NUMBER()` over an aggregate and chained LEFT JOINs are standard and expected to work, but the union design in this same PR compiled cleanly and was refused by an engine. **Live Snowflake + Unity Catalog verification is yours to run before #327 is considered fully verified.** Until then the fallback is the safety net: worst case is current performance, not a broken profiler.</result>

## PR

**#1325** — https://github.com/TheurgicDuke771/DataQ/pull/1325
`feat: scale-aware execution — sampling + partition batching + OOM guardrail for flat-file/UC runners (#595)` · `Fixes #595` · milestone *v1.1 Week 6* · 8 commits · **all 16 CI checks pass** on head `56b3e311`.

## Design choices

**Where the spec lives** — on the suite's run-target JSONB (`{"sampling": {"strategy": "head"|"random", "rows": N, "seed": ?}}`), so no migration for the config side. `SampleSpec` sits in `datasources/base.py` beside `BatchSpec`; behaviour is a new pure module `datasources/sampling.py` (100% covered).

**Where sampled-ness is stored** — new nullable `results.sampling` JSONB (migration `4d23b47ee564`, up/down tested against Postgres), returned by `GET /runs/{id}` unredacted (it carries counts, not target data). **Per-result, not per-run**: within one run a volume monitor pushes down (exact) while the expectations beside it saw 100k of 5M — a run-level flag would have to lie about one. `sampled` is stored explicitly, so a "sample" larger than the dataset reports as the complete read it is instead of crying wolf on every small target. `null` = complete read, which is also what every pre-existing row means — no backfill.

**Caps** — `RUN_MAX_SCAN_BYTES` (128 MiB, flat files) and `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS` (1.5M, UC). `0` disables the cap *and* its probe. Sampling **replaces** the cap rather than stacking with it.

**What UC pushes down** — freshness/volume were already scalar SQL aggregates and `schema_drift` already read `information_schema` (verified, unchanged). The gap was the *expectation* read: now `LIMIT rows+1` (head) or `TABLESAMPLE (p PERCENT) … LIMIT rows` sized from `COUNT(*)` (random). Not `ORDER BY rand()` (global sort) and not `TABLESAMPLE (n ROWS)` (Spark implements it as a plain LIMIT — a head sample wearing a random label).

Sampling is **refused at save time** on Snowflake/Iceberg rather than ignored, and never applied to freshness (a MAX over a sample is a *smaller* maximum → healthy data reported critically stale).

## Measurements (docs/perf-baseline.md §W6)

5M-row order-lines, real runner, five expectations. Floor 329 MiB.

| Object | Mode | Outcome | Wall | Peak RSS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| CSV 249 MB | full, cap off | 5/5 pass | 4.26 s | **2,210 MiB** |
| CSV 249 MB | full, cap on | **refused** | **0.00 s** | 329 MiB |
| CSV 249 MB | head 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 0.15 s | **411 MiB** |
| CSV 249 MB | random 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 1.98 s | **550 MiB** |
| Parquet 114 MB | full, cap off | 5/5 pass | 2.11 s | 1,290 MiB |
| Parquet 114 MB | head/random 100k | 5/5, `sampled: true` | 0.10/0.18 s | **405/468 MiB** |

The measurement earned its keep: **my first 256 MiB default was wrong** — that 249 MB CSV passes it and still OOMs. 128 MiB comes from the measured ~8–9× bytes→RSS expansion and lands on the W3 pass/fail boundary.

## Tests

**4056 passed / 1 skipped, 97.22% coverage.** `sampling.py` 100%, `unity_catalog.py` 99%, `flatfile.py` 98%. Black/Ruff/mypy/Bandit all clean locally before push.

Three real defects found by my own tests/measurements and fixed: `take_head` pulled one batch past its limit (a wasted range request on the path that exists to be cheap); the cap default; and a size probe that fired even when the cap was disabled.

## Deferred

- **Live UC verification pending (orchestrator)** — `TABLESAMPLE`'s behaviour is a Databricks fact; per #953 only a live run is evidence. The SQL DataQ builds is unit-pinned; the flat-file half is measured.
- Iceberg sampling (excluded rather than half-supported), column projection for flat-file monitors, and incremental/delta-only validation (out of scope by design — a design note is in §W6: a watermark belongs beside `sampling` with the same result-record shape).
- UI surfacing is the #318 batch's; the API returns everything a badge needs.

One process note worth carrying: an unstubbed UC count probe doesn't *fail* a test — it opens a real Databricks session to the fake host and retries for 15 minutes, so the suite reports a timeout instead of a defect. That cost me one 921 s test run before I found it; both affected tests now stub it with a comment saying why.</result>

## /code-review — 7-angle fan-out, consolidated (high effort)

**Verdict: request changes.** The architecture (SampleSpec on the run-target, per-result `sampling` record, refuse-don't-ignore at save time, freshness exemption) is right, and the measurements are honest. But the fan-out found six correctness defects — three on the feature's own headline path — plus two coverage gaps that reintroduce the exact failure classes this PR exists to close.

### Must-fix (correctness)

**C1 — TABLESAMPLE percent formats in scientific notation on large tables.** `unity_catalog.py:360`: the percent is interpolated via Python float repr, which flips to scientific below 1e-4 — and Databricks accepts only INTEGER/DECIMAL literals. `random rows=100` on a 200M-row table emits `TABLESAMPLE (6e-05 PERCENT)` → PARSE_SYNTAX_ERROR; even the `_MIN_SAMPLE_PERCENT` floor renders as `1e-06`. The very-large-table case — the reason this feature exists — fails deterministically. Fix: fixed-point formatting (e.g. `f"{percent:.6f}"` with a floor that survives it).

**C2 — UC `seed` is accepted, stamped on the result, and never used.** `unity_catalog.py:358`: the docs promise "add seed to make a run reproducible", `parse_sample_spec` accepts seed for random, and `sampling_record` persists it — but the emitted SQL has no `REPEATABLE(seed)`, so consecutive runs draw different rows while the result claims reproducibility. Emit `REPEATABLE(seed)` or refuse seed on UC; do not stamp what wasn't honored.

**C3 — empty Bernoulli draw → vacuous all-green.** `unity_catalog.py:373`: for small `rows`, P(zero rows) is material (~30% at expected 1.2 rows); an empty frame passes every column expectation vacuously with `rows=0, sampled=true` and a green run — the "all-green on no rows" outcome the `_MIN_SAMPLE_PERCENT` comment promises can't happen. Guard the result: empty (or grossly short) sampled frame → `error`/`skip` with a DataQ-authored message, or re-draw with a raised percent.

**C4 — CSV head window cut is not quote-aware.** `flatfile.py:599`: the window is cut at the last raw `\n`; on CSVs with quoted fields containing newlines the cut can land inside quotes → pandas `ParserError` ("EOF inside string") or silent tail mis-parse — on files the full read handles fine, intermittently by layout. `csv_row_count` uses pyarrow precisely because a newline is not a row boundary; the head path needs the same property (pyarrow-based head, or quote-aware trim).

**C5 — dry-run swallows `ScanTooLargeError` into the generic message.** `dryrun_service.py:218`: the blanket `except` classifies it → "dry run could not execute", with no cap size and no "set a sampling strategy" remedy — while this PR's own comment says the preview must refuse for the same reason. Fix alongside **C6**: `run_service._failure_reason` special-cases `ScanTooLargeError` by isinstance, but the codebase already has the marker for exactly this — `SafeMonitorError` (which `ScanTooLargeError` subclasses), already trusted verbatim at `monitors.py:761` and `anomaly.py:385`. One shared `safe_failure_reason(exc)` helper branching on `SafeMonitorError` serves run + dry-run with one policy instead of a third, narrower copy.

**C6 — table-row-count expectations silently measure the sample.** `flatfile.py:1065`: `expect_table_row_count_to_be_between` against a sampled frame deterministically observes the sample size — a healthy 5M-row file with `min_value=4M` fails critically forever (and the inverse passes wrongly). Monitors were exempted for exactly this smaller-aggregate reason; row-count expectations weren't. Mirror the freshness treatment: refuse the combination at save time (and at run time for pre-existing suites), with a clear message.

**C7 — the comparison path accepts a `sampling` block and silently drops it.** `comparison_run.py:69` / `check_service.py:479`: a comparison check's `source` goes through `resolve_target`, which now validates and ACCEPTS `sampling` — then `DatasetSpec` drops it. Save succeeds, the author believes the read is bounded, the run materializes everything. This is precisely the "silently-dropped sampling block" failure the registry docstring says the 422 exists to prevent. Fix: refuse `sampling` in comparison source specs at save time (threading it through DatasetReader is follow-up scale).

**C8 — MCP read surface can't say "passed on a sample".** `mcp/server.py:234`: `get_suite_results` builds its payload by hand and wasn't extended with `sampling` — an AI client confidently reports full-dataset quality from a 2% sample, the #424/#1115 overclaim class reintroduced for every MCP consumer. Add the field.

### Fix-or-file (judgment call, but every one dispositioned)

**J1 — mutable-object two-pass random (flatfile):** `row_count()` then a second stream; a re-uploaded landing-zone file between passes yields a silently short/skewed sample with a stale `total_rows`. Cheap honesty fix: compare rows-walked vs counted total and refuse/annotate on mismatch (ETag pin is the deluxe version).
**J2 — `dataset_reader.py:219` flat-file comparison read is uncapped** — downloads the whole object before its row-cap check, so the #755 OOM survives via any comparison on an oversized object, and the PR's config comment ("never the current behaviour") overclaims. The preflight it says doesn't exist now does (`file_stat`). Apply the byte-cap preflight there, or correct the claim and file.
**J3 — Iceberg runner is a third full-load runner with no probe, no cap, no sampling** — `RUN_MAX_SCAN_ROWS` claims to govern materialization but skips one of three materializing runners; #755 stays open there. Sampling exclusion was deliberate and fine; the cap wasn't. Cheap version: `scan().count()` probe + row cap refusal. In-PR or file with explicit AC.
**J4 — sample ≥ total degenerate case:** `sampling.py:144` returns `list(range(total))` (~40MB for 1.4M rows) and `take_indices` gather-copies every batch — for a "sample" that changes nothing. Skip selection when `rows >= total`.
**J5 — capability set vs `**_` swallow:** `SAMPLING_CAPABLE_TYPES` (registry) is uncoupled from whether a builder actually threads `sampling`; `_snowflake_runner`/`_iceberg_runner` swallow it via `**_`. A test asserting set-membership ⇔ kwarg-threading (or a runner-level `supports_sampling`) closes the add-to-set-forget-the-builder trap.

### File as follow-ups (structural, not this PR)

**P2 — a column literally named `freq` silently returns fewer top values.** `profile_service.py:340`: the derived table renders `count(*) AS freq … ORDER BY count(*) DESC, freq LIMIT n`. PG/Snowflake resolve the bare `freq` in ORDER BY to the OUTPUT alias (= the count, i.e. no tie-break), while `row_number() OVER (… , freq)` resolves it to the INPUT column — so the LIMIT keeps a tie-set that disagrees with the rank, kept rows can carry `rn > top_n` (join nothing, vanish), and the profile shows fewer values than exist, no error, no fallback. **P3 — the try-block swallows our own reader's bugs into permanent silent degradation.** `profile_service.py:665`: the catch wraps `collect_batched_top_values` (pure Python) too, so a shipped reader defect silently routes every profile through the N+1 path forever, with one warning nobody alerts on — #327 un-fixed in practice while all tests stay green. Catch `SQLAlchemyError`/`DBAPIError` around the execute only.

**P4 — MCP `profile_column` has unbounded `top_n` that now controls statement size.** `mcp/server.py:533`: no `ge/le` (the REST endpoint has `ge=1 le=100`), and the rank driver materializes `top_n` UNION-ALL branches per chunk — `top_n=100000` compiles a multi-MB CompoundSelect in the request thread. LLM-generated args are exactly the callers that do this. Bound it to match REST.

**P5 — all-or-nothing fallback regresses the pre-PR ceiling.** `profile_service.py:664`: chunk 2 of 2 failing discards chunk 1's results and re-runs ALL columns per-column — 53 round-trips where pre-#327 cost 51, with 25 columns computed twice against the warehouse that just proved slow. - **m1** `top_n < 1` branch: routes to per-column LIMIT-0 queries (N round-trips returning nothing, for an input both API surfaces make unreachable) — `return {}` / `{col: []}` with zero queries.
- **m2** Test fake substring routing: `if col in sql` cross-wires `c1` ↔ `c10`/`c11` if the fallback loop is ever reached — anchor the match (word boundary / `WHERE <col> IS NOT NULL` regex).

- **m4** Compose the batched builder FROM `build_top_values_query` (+ `.add_columns(row_number…)`) so "exactly the per-column query plus a rank" is true by construction, retiring the fragment-matching drift test.
- **m5** Consider `sqlalchemy.values()` for the rank driver instead of a top_n-branch UNION ALL (compact `(VALUES …)` rendering, no type-unification concern) — fold into the live verification below, not a separate pass.

### Carried to live verification (orchestrator, pre-merge)
Per the #953 rule: batched SQL proven on Postgres only. The live Snowflake + UC pass must check (a) correctness of the rank-join, (b) **timing vs the per-column path** — `_TOP_VALUES_BATCH=25` is calibrated on the Postgres planner (the GEQO-at-12-relations cliff is PG machinery); if the warehouses' cliff sits lower, the batch could be slower than the N+1 it replaces with zero signal, since success doesn't trigger the fallback.

Single-element `union_all` compiles for top_n=1; `folding_identifier` quotes without lowercasing so the fake's lookups match; omitted empty-column keys safe (`assemble_profile.get(col, [])` is the sole consumer); dialect/catalog threading identical to the removed inline path; lowercase `rn`/`v_0`/`f_0` labels follow the proven `nulls_0` normalization precedent; columns named `rn`/`value` benign; fallback warning logs exception type only (no SQL/values — PII-clean).

# Local DataQ ⟷ prod mirror — session summary + runbook

**Session: 2026-08-03.** DataQ's local dev stack was converted into a live
mirror of prod (real secrets, real connections/suites, real datasource
traffic) and the local harness stack (this repo's `local/`) was brought up
alongside it. This doc is the replication runbook for redoing that, plus
guidance on using the mirror day-to-day and on actually exercising the local
Airflow/MinIO stack (which, as of this session, sits up but **unused** — see
§4).

Companion: DataQ's own memory note
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-arijit-Coding-Python-DataQ/memory/project_local_prod_mirror_setup.md`
carries the same gotchas for AI-assistant sessions; this file is the
human-readable, repo-anchored version.

---

## 1. What was done this session

1. **Brought up DataQ's own compose stack** (`docker compose up -d` in
   `~/Coding/Python/DataQ`) — postgres/redis/openbao/mailpit/api/worker/frontend,
   all default services.
2. **Brought up this repo's local harness** (`local/harness_local.sh up`) —
   Airflow (Postgres+Redis+CeleryExecutor) + MinIO, joined onto DataQ's
   compose network.
3. **Configured multi-user email-OTP sign-in** by setting `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL`
   in DataQ's root `.env` — see the gotcha in §2.2, this is the ONE switch,
   not a separately-settable allowlist.
4. **Mirrored local OpenBao onto Azure Key Vault exactly** — purged 143
   unrelated stale secrets from a prior local session, wrote in the 25 real
   `dataq-app-kv-aw6laj` secrets by name (values piped directly between `az`
   and OpenBao's HTTP API, never printed or written to disk), verified the
   name sets are now identical.
5. **Replaced local DB seed/demo data with prod's real `users` /
   `connections` / `suites` / `checks`** — nuked the local schema, re-ran
   migrations, opened a **temporary** Postgres firewall rule, copied the four
   tables straight from prod via `psycopg2`, closed the firewall rule
   immediately after. 13 connections, 12 suites, 30 checks, 8 users.
6. **Verified functionality**: OTP sign-in end-to-end (Mailpit), suite runs
   across Snowflake / ADLS flat-file / Unity Catalog (all green, including a
   deliberately-seeded prod failure behaving as expected) / Iceberg (failed —
   see §2.5, expected given the closed firewall rule).
7. **Backfilled asset resolution** — the raw DB copy bypassed the service
   layer that normally creates an `assets` row on suite save, so `GET
   /assets` was empty. Fixed by re-`PATCH`ing each suite with its own
   existing `target`, which forces `resolve_and_upsert_asset` without
   changing anything else. 10 assets now exist, correctly deduplicated.
8. **Reset a latent lineage-sync landmine** — the copied Unity Catalog
   connections carried prod's *incremental* lineage watermark
   (`2026-07-27`) into a local DB whose `lineage_edges` table was never
   copied. Left alone, a future local warehouse-lineage refresh would have
   silently started from that stale cursor and permanently skipped
   everything before it. Reset `lineage_watermark` /
   `lineage_last_refresh_at` / `lineage_last_tier` to `NULL` on both UC
   connections.

**Not done (deliberately out of scope):** `trigger_bindings` / `schedules` /
`suite_notifications` / access-grants were not copied from prod — local
suites won't auto-fire on a cron or an orchestration trigger. Lineage edges
themselves were not copied and are not backfilled (they only populate via a
live refresh, which is off locally by default — same as prod).

---

## 2. Replication runbook (redo this from scratch)

Run this in `~/Coding/Python/DataQ` unless noted. Requires `az` logged in
with Key Vault read + Container App secret read + the shared Postgres
server's firewall-rule permissions (deployer/`dataq-admin`-tier access).

### 2.1 Bring up both stacks

```bash
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ
docker compose up -d                       # postgres/redis/openbao/mailpit/api/worker/frontend

cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ-harness/local
./harness_local.sh up                      # requires DataQ's stack up first (joins dataq_default)
```

### 2.2 Multi-user OTP sign-in

`.env`'s `DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL` **is** the allowlist — `docker-compose.yml`
wires it straight into `AUTH_OTP_ALLOWED_EMAILS` verbatim
(`${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL?...}`, not a separate override). Comma-separate it for
multiple users:

```bash
# .env is deliberately unwritable by the Edit tool in an AI session (secrets
# guard) — append with a shell redirect instead:
printf 'DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL=you@example.com,teammate@example.com\n' >> .env
docker compose up -d api worker             # env is a start-time snapshot
```

`WORKSPACE_ADMIN_EMAILS` defaults to `dev-bypass@dataq.local,${DATAQ_SIGNIN_EMAIL}`
— so every signed-in address is workspace-admin by default, which is what
gives a freshly-provisioned local user visibility into prod's suites (they
belong to prod's *user rows*, not to whichever new email you sign in with;
workspace-admin has implicit visibility into everything, ADR 0027).

### 2.3 Mirror OpenBao onto Key Vault (exact set, no extras)

```bash
KV=dataq-app-kv-aw6laj   # re-verify with `az keyvault list` in case it's been renamed
source .env.app          # OPENBAO_ADDR / OPENBAO_MOUNT / OPENBAO_TOKEN

az keyvault secret list --vault-name "$KV" --query "[?attributes.enabled].name" -o tsv | sort > /tmp/kv_names.txt

curl -s -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata?list=true" \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; print('\n'.join(sorted(json.load(sys.stdin)['data']['keys'])))" > /tmp/local_names.txt

# purge anything local-only
comm -23 /tmp/local_names.txt /tmp/kv_names.txt | while read -r n; do
  curl -s -o /dev/null -X DELETE -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/metadata/$n"
done

# write in every KV secret (value piped straight through, never echoed/printed)
while read -r n; do
  az keyvault secret show --vault-name "$KV" --name "$n" --query value -o tsv \
    | python3 -c "import sys,json; print(json.dumps({'data':{'value': sys.stdin.readline().rstrip(chr(10))}}))" \
    | curl -s -o /dev/null -X POST -H "X-Vault-Token: $OPENBAO_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
      --data-binary @- "$OPENBAO_ADDR/v1/$OPENBAO_MOUNT/data/$n"
done < /tmp/kv_names.txt
```

**Gotcha:** this purge also deletes `dataq-local-smtp` — the bundled Mailpit
catcher's password, seeded locally by the one-shot `otp-mail-secret` compose
service. It never exists in prod Key Vault by design (prod mails via Gmail
SMTP under different secret names), so a strict "match KV exactly" diff
always removes it, and OTP sign-in then fails with
`otp_email_not_configured`. Fix, every time:

```bash
docker compose up -d --force-recreate otp-mail-secret
```

### 2.4 Wipe local seed data, pull in prod's real data

```bash
cd ~/Coding/Python/DataQ

# 1. temp access to the shared prod Postgres server
MYIP=$(curl -s https://api.ipify.org)
az postgres flexible-server firewall-rule create -g dataq-rg --server-name dataq-pg-wus3-3erlgd \
  --name "temp-local-sync-$(python3 -c 'import time;print(int(time.time()))')" \
  --start-ip-address "$MYIP" --end-ip-address "$MYIP"

# 2. resolve prod's DATABASE_URL — it is NOT in any tfvars file (apply-time-only var);
#    read it straight off the live Container App secret instead:
export PROD_DATABASE_URL=$(az containerapp secret list -n dataq-app-api -g dataq-rg --show-values -o json \
  | python3 -c "import json,sys; d=json.load(sys.stdin); print(next(s['value'] for s in d if s['name']=='database-url'))")

# 3. nuke local schema, re-migrate (NO reseed — that's exactly the demo data being removed)
docker compose exec -T postgres psql -U dataq -d dataq -c "DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public;"
export LOCAL_DATABASE_URL="REDACTED"
(cd backend && DATABASE_URL="$LOCAL_DATABASE_URL" conda run -n dataq alembic upgrade head)
# Gotcha: `conda run -n dataq sh -c "cd backend && alembic upgrade head"` alone fails with
# "no password supplied" — pydantic-settings' env_file=".env.app" resolves relative to cwd,
# and there is no backend/.env.app (only the repo-root one). Export DATABASE_URL explicitly.

"""Live verification of PR #1323's batched top-values SQL vs Snowflake + UC.

Runs the PR-branch code (agent worktree) against the REAL warehouses via the
local mirror DB's connection rows + OpenBao secrets. Per the #953 rule.

Checks per warehouse:
  1. Batched path == per-column path (values AND types), via the production
     functions themselves.
  2. Timing: batched vs per-column wall clock (the GEQO-cliff concern).
  3. The full profile_table() production entry point succeeds.

Never prints secret values. Prints only table/column names, counts, timings,
equality verdicts.
"""

import os
import sys
import time

WORKTREE = "/Users/arijit/Coding/Python/DataQ/.claude/worktrees/agent-a22d75afd904f1655"
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.join(WORKTREE, "backend"))

os.environ["DATABASE_URL"] = "REDACTED"

from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text  # noqa: E402
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session  # noqa: E402

from app.core.secrets import get_secret_store  # noqa: E402
from app.db.models import Connection  # noqa: E402
from app.services import profile_service  # noqa: E402
from app.services.profile_service import (  # noqa: E402
    _fetch_top_values,
    _open_connection,
    _top_values_per_column,
    profile_table,
)

TARGETS = {
    "snowflake": {"table": "ORDERS_HEADER", "schema": "RETAIL", "catalog": None},
    "unity_catalog": {
        "table": "feedback_sentiment",
        "schema": "gold",
        "catalog": "dataq_retail",
    },
}

TOP_N = 10


def columns_for(conn, dialect_name, schema, table, catalog):
    if dialect_name == "snowflake":
        q = text(
            "SELECT column_name FROM information_schema.columns "
            "WHERE table_schema = :s AND table_name = :t ORDER BY ordinal_position"
        )
        rows = conn.execute(q, {"s": schema, "t": table}).fetchall()
    else:
        q = text(
            f"SELECT column_name FROM {catalog}.information_schema.columns "
            "WHERE table_schema = :s AND table_name = :t ORDER BY ordinal_position"
        )
        rows = conn.execute(q, {"s": schema, "t": table}).fetchall()
    return [r[0] for r in rows]


def norm(d):
    return {k: [(str(v), int(c)) for v, c in vals] for k, vals in d.items()}


def main() -> int:
    app_engine = create_engine(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
    store = get_secret_store()
    failures = 0

    with Session(app_engine) as session:
        conns = (
            session.query(Connection)
            .filter(Connection.type.in_(list(TARGETS)))
            .all()
        )
        by_type = {c.type: c for c in conns}

        for ctype, tgt in TARGETS.items():
            connection = by_type.get(ctype)
            if connection is None:
                print(f"[{ctype}] NO CONNECTION ROW — skip")
                failures += 1
                continue
            print(f"\n=== {ctype}: {connection.name} -> "
                  f"{tgt['catalog'] or ''}.{tgt['schema']}.{tgt['table']} ===")
            try:
                with _open_connection(connection, store) as conn:
                    dialect = conn.dialect
                    cols = columns_for(
                        conn, dialect.name, tgt["schema"], tgt["table"], tgt["catalog"]
                    )
                    print(f"columns ({len(cols)}): {cols}")

                    t0 = time.perf_counter()
                    per_col = _top_values_per_column(
                        conn,
                        schema=tgt["schema"],
                        table=tgt["table"],
                        columns=cols,
                        top_n=TOP_N,
                        catalog=tgt["catalog"],
                        dialect=dialect,
                    )
                    t_per = time.perf_counter() - t0

                    t0 = time.perf_counter()
                    batched = _fetch_top_values(
                        conn,
                        schema=tgt["schema"],
                        table=tgt["table"],
                        columns=cols,
                        top_n=TOP_N,
                        catalog=tgt["catalog"],
                        dialect=dialect,
                    )
                    t_bat = time.perf_counter() - t0

                    equal = norm(per_col) == norm(batched)
                    print(f"equivalence (values+counts, {len(cols)} cols): "
                          f"{'PASS' if equal else 'FAIL'}")
                    if not equal:
                        failures += 1
                        for c in cols:
                            a, b = norm(per_col).get(c), norm(batched).get(c)
                            if a != b:
                                print(f"  DIFF {c}: per-column={a} batched={b}")
                    # type fidelity: compare python types positionally
                    tmatch = all(
                        [type(v).__name__ for v, _ in per_col.get(c, [])]
                        == [type(v).__name__ for v, _ in batched.get(c, [])]
                        for c in cols
                    )
                    print(f"type fidelity: {'PASS' if tmatch else 'FAIL'}")
                    if not tmatch:
                        failures += 1
                    print(
                        f"timing: per-column {t_per:.2f}s ({len(cols)} round-trips) "
                        f"vs batched {t_bat:.2f}s "
                        f"({(len(cols) + 24) // 25 + 0} chunk round-trip(s)) "
                        f"-> {'batched FASTER' if t_bat < t_per else 'batched SLOWER'}"
                    )
                    if t_bat > t_per:
                        print("  WARNING: batched slower than per-column on this "
                              "warehouse — the GEQO-cliff concern")

                # 3. full production entry point
                t0 = time.perf_counter()
                result = profile_table(
                    connection,
                    table=tgt["table"],
                    schema=tgt["schema"],
                    columns=cols[: min(len(cols), 50)],
                    top_n=TOP_N,
                    secret_store=store,
                    catalog=tgt["catalog"],
                )
                t_full = time.perf_counter() - t0
                ncols = len(result.columns)
                n_top = sum(1 for c in result.columns if c.top_values)
                print(f"profile_table: OK — {ncols} column profiles, "
                      f"{n_top} with top_values, {t_full:.2f}s total")
            except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
                failures += 1
                print(f"[{ctype}] FAILED: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

    print(f"\n{'ALL PASS' if failures == 0 else f'{failures} FAILURE(S)'}")
    return 1 if failures else 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

def _recover_transaction(conn: Any) -> None:
    """Roll back so the fallback can run on a usable connection (#327 review, P1).

    A server-side rejection of the batched statement leaves SQLAlchemy's autobegun
    transaction **aborted** on Postgres-family engines: every subsequent statement
    on that connection raises ``InFailedSqlTransaction`` until it is rolled back.
    Without this the fallback was dead code exactly when it was needed — the
    profile 502'd where the pre-#327 per-column path would have succeeded. Not
    theoretical: reproduced against a live Postgres, and pinned by a test that
    executes a genuinely failing statement rather than raising from Python.

    Best-effort by design. The profiler only ever reads, so there is nothing to
    lose by rolling back, and a connection object that cannot (a test double, an
    autocommit-only driver) must not turn a recoverable batch failure into a hard
    one — hence the broad catch and the log instead of a raise.
    """
    try:
        conn.rollback()
    except Exception as exc:
        log.warning("profile_top_values_rollback_failed", error_type=type(exc).__name__)


def _fetch_top_values(

from sqlalchemy.orm import Session
from backend.app.core.secrets import get_secret_store
from backend.app.db.models import Connection
from backend.app.datasources.sampling import SampleSpec, SAMPLE_HEAD, SAMPLE_RANDOM
from backend.app.datasources.unity_catalog import (
    build_unity_catalog_runner, format_sample_percent)
from backend.app.datasources.base import CheckSpec

TABLE, SCHEMA, CATALOG = "feedback_sentiment", "gold", "dataq_retail"
fails = 0

def check(label, cond, detail=""):
    global fails
    print(f"{'PASS' if cond else 'FAIL'}  {label}{': ' + detail if detail else ''}")
    if not cond:
        fails += 1

engine = create_engine(os.environ["DATABASE_URL"])
store = get_secret_store()
with Session(engine) as session:
    conn_row = session.query(Connection).filter_by(type="unity_catalog").one()

def runner_with(spec):
    return build_unity_catalog_runner(
        config=conn_row.config, secret_ref=conn_row.secret_ref,
        secret_store=store, catalog=CATALOG, sampling=spec)

# 1. head
r = runner_with(SampleSpec(strategy=SAMPLE_HEAD, rows=50))
frame, record = r._load_frame(table=TABLE, schema=SCHEMA)
check("head 50: frame rows == 50", len(frame) == 50, f"got {len(frame)}")
check("head 50: record.sampled true", record is not None and record.get("sampled") is True, str(record))

# 2. random (no seed)
r = runner_with(SampleSpec(strategy=SAMPLE_RANDOM, rows=50))
frame, record = r._load_frame(table=TABLE, schema=SCHEMA)
check("random 50: TABLESAMPLE parsed + drew rows", len(frame) > 0, f"got {len(frame)} rows")
check("random 50: record sampled+strategy", record is not None and record.get("strategy") == "random", str(record))

# 3. random + seed, twice
ids = []
for i in range(2):
    r = runner_with(SampleSpec(strategy=SAMPLE_RANDOM, rows=50, seed=7))
    frame, record = r._load_frame(table=TABLE, schema=SCHEMA)
    ids.append(sorted(frame["feedback_id"].astype(str).tolist()))
check("random seed=7: REPEATABLE parsed", len(ids[0]) > 0)
check("random seed=7: two draws identical", ids[0] == ids[1],
      f"{len(ids[0])} vs {len(ids[1])} rows, equal={ids[0] == ids[1]}")

# 4. tiny-percent literal (C1 regression shape) as a direct statement
lit = format_sample_percent(0.0001)
check("format_sample_percent(0.0001) fixed-point", lit == "0.000100", lit)
eng = r._build_engine()
with eng.connect() as c:
    n = c.execute(text(
        f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE} "
        f"TABLESAMPLE ({lit} PERCENT) REPEATABLE (7)")).scalar()
    check("tiny literal parses live", n is not None, f"count={n}")
    floor_lit = format_sample_percent(0.000001)
    n2 = c.execute(text(
        f"SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {CATALOG}.{SCHEMA}.{TABLE} "
        f"TABLESAMPLE ({floor_lit} PERCENT)")).scalar()
    check(f"floor literal ({floor_lit}) parses live", n2 is not None, f"count={n2}")
eng.dispose()

# 5. full run_checks with sampling
r = runner_with(SampleSpec(strategy=SAMPLE_HEAD, rows=100))
t0 = time.perf_counter()
outcome = r.run_checks(
    table=TABLE, schema=SCHEMA,
    checks=[CheckSpec(name="rating not null", type="expect_column_values_to_not_be_null",
                      column="rating", kwargs={}),

                      column="sentiment",

dt = time.perf_counter() - t0

check("run_checks: 2 outcomes", len(outcome.checks) == 2,

check("run_checks: sampling stamped on every result",
      all(s is not None and s.get("sampled") is True for s in recs), str(recs[:1]))

print(f"\n{'ALL PASS' if fails == 0 else f'{fails} FAILURE(S)'}")
raise SystemExit(1 if fails else 0)

Sampled-ness lands on `results.sampling` (new nullable JSONB) per **check**, not per run — a volume monitor pushes down and is exact while the expectations beside it saw 100k of 5M, and one flag would have to lie about one of them; `sampled` is explicit, so a "sample" covering the whole dataset is reported as the complete read it is. Sampling is **refused at save time** on Snowflake/Iceberg and never applied to freshness (a MAX over a sample is a smaller maximum → healthy data reported critically stale). Measured, §W6 of [perf-baseline.md](perf-baseline.md): a 249 MB / 5M-row CSV needs **2,210 MiB** uncapped, is refused in **0.00 s** capped, and runs at **411 MiB / 0.15 s** sampled. The first cap draft (256 MiB) was wrong and the measurement is what caught it — that CSV passes it and still OOMs. **Live UC verification done 2026-08-14** (the #953 rule): head + random draws live, `TABLESAMPLE (p PERCENT)` fixed-point literals down to the `0.000001` floor parse, `REPEATABLE(7)` reproduced identical 50-row draws twice, and a live `run_checks` stamped `sampling` on every result | Theme 7 / G-b |

Rank driver LEFT-joined to one derived table per column, chunked at 25 (measured: a single 50-way join costs 3x a 25-way one, Postgres switches to its genetic optimiser at 12 relations).
